claim: Proteomic analysis showed a higher abundance of fibromodulin (FMOD) in the conditioned medium of differentiated glioma cells (DGCs) compared to that of glioma stem-like cells (GSCs).
source: Proteomic analysis showed a higher abundance of the extracellular matrix small leucine-rich proteoglycan fibromodulin (FMOD) in the conditioned medium of differentiated glioma cells (DGCs), the equivalent of glioma non-CSCs, compared to that of glioma stem-like cells (GSCs).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from quantitative proteomics using nano-LC-FT-MS/MS and label-free quantification as described in the manuscript.

claim: DGCs silenced for FMOD fail to cooperate with co-implanted GSCs to promote tumor growth.
source: DGCs silenced for FMOD fail to cooperate with co-implanted GSCs to promote tumor growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from co-implantation experiments in a syngeneic mouse model using DBT-Luc glioma cells.

claim: FMOD downregulation does not affect GSC growth and differentiation in vitro.
source: FMOD downregulation neither affects GSC growth and differentiation nor DGC growth and reprogramming in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from neurosphere assays, limiting dilution assays, and differentiation experiments using multiple glioma cell lines.

claim: FMOD downregulation does not affect DGC growth and reprogramming in vitro.
source: FMOD downregulation neither affects GSC growth and differentiation nor DGC growth and reprogramming in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from reprogramming assays and neurosphere formation assays using multiple glioma cell lines.

claim: DGC-secreted FMOD promotes angiogenesis by activating integrin-dependent Notch signaling in endothelial cells.
source: DGC-secreted FMOD promotes angiogenesis by activating integrin-dependent Notch signaling in endothelial cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro angiogenesis assays, RPPA analysis, luciferase reporter assays, and Western blotting experiments.

claim: Conditional silencing of FMOD in newly generated DGCs in vivo inhibits the growth of GSC-initiated tumors due to poorly developed vasculature.
source: Furthermore, conditional silencing of FMOD in newly generated DGCs in vivo inhibits the growth of GSC-initiated tumors due to poorly developed vasculature and increases mouse survival.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from intracranial orthotopic mouse glioma models using AGR53-GSC, DBT-Luc-GSC, and MGG8-GSC cells with doxycycline-inducible FMOD silencing.

claim: Conditional silencing of FMOD in newly generated DGCs in vivo increases mouse survival.
source: Furthermore, conditional silencing of FMOD in newly generated DGCs in vivo inhibits the growth of GSC-initiated tumors due to poorly developed vasculature and increases mouse survival.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Kaplan-Meier survival analysis in intracranial orthotopic mouse glioma models.

claim: 119 proteins are more abundant in GSC conditioned medium compared to DGC conditioned medium.
source: We found that 119 proteins are more abundant in GSC CM, while 185 proteins are more abundant in the DGC CM (p<0.05, Figure 1A; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative proteomic data from nano-LC-FT-MS/MS analysis with label-free quantification.

claim: 185 proteins are more abundant in DGC conditioned medium compared to GSC conditioned medium.
source: We found that 119 proteins are more abundant in GSC CM, while 185 proteins are more abundant in the DGC CM (p<0.05, Figure 1A; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative proteomic data from nano-LC-FT-MS/MS analysis with label-free quantification.

claim: DGC conditioned medium is enriched in proteins with extracellular or cell surface localization.
source: Analysis of overrepresented functional categories among proteins exhibiting differential abundances in GSC vs. DGC CMs using Perseus with a p-value <0.05 revealed that the DGC CM is enriched in proteins known to exhibit extracellular or cell surface localization, such as proteins annotated as ECM organization while terms related to DNA replication and many signaling pathways are enriched in GSC CM (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Gene Ontology analysis of proteomic data using Perseus software.

claim: GSC conditioned medium is enriched in proteins related to DNA replication and many signaling pathways.
source: Analysis of overrepresented functional categories among proteins exhibiting differential abundances in GSC vs. DGC CMs using Perseus with a p-value <0.05 revealed that the DGC CM is enriched in proteins known to exhibit extracellular or cell surface localization, such as proteins annotated as ECM organization while terms related to DNA replication and many signaling pathways are enriched in GSC CM (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Gene Ontology analysis of proteomic data using Perseus software.

claim: FMOD exhibits the highest DGC CM/GSC CM protein ratio among ECM proteoglycans.
source: We thus focused on FMOD, which exhibited the highest DGC CM/GSC CM protein ratio.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative proteomic data showing FMOD has the highest ratio among six ECM proteoglycans identified.

claim: FMOD is upregulated in GBM due to the loss of promoter methylation orchestrated by TGF-β1-dependent epigenetic regulation.
source: FMOD is a small leucine-rich repeat proteoglycan upregulated in GBM due to the loss of promoter methylation orchestrated by TGF-β1-dependent epigenetic regulation (Mondal et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Mondal et al., 2017.

claim: FMOD promotes glioma cell migration through actin cytoskeleton remodeling mediated by an integrin-FAK-Src-Rho-ROCK signaling pathway.
source: FMOD promotes glioma cell migration through actin cytoskeleton remodeling mediated by an integrin-FAK-Src-Rho-ROCK signaling pathway but does not affect colony-forming ability, growth on soft agar, chemosensitivity, and glioma cell proliferation (Mondal et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Mondal et al., 2017.

claim: FMOD does not affect colony-forming ability, growth on soft agar, chemosensitivity, and glioma cell proliferation.
source: FMOD promotes glioma cell migration through actin cytoskeleton remodeling mediated by an integrin-FAK-Src-Rho-ROCK signaling pathway but does not affect colony-forming ability, growth on soft agar, chemosensitivity, and glioma cell proliferation (Mondal et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Mondal et al., 2017.

claim: FMOD transcript levels are significantly higher in DGCs compared to GSCs in MGG4, MGG6, and MGG8 cell lines.
source: We first confirmed the higher abundance of FMOD seen in DGC CM compared to GSC CM (Figure 1C) both at the transcript level (Figure 1D) and at the protein level (Figure 1E and F) in three GSC cell lines (MGG4, MGG6, and MGG8).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: FMOD protein levels are higher in DGCs compared to GSCs in MGG4, MGG6, and MGG8 cell lines.
source: We first confirmed the higher abundance of FMOD seen in DGC CM compared to GSC CM (Figure 1C) both at the transcript level (Figure 1D) and at the protein level (Figure 1E and F) in three GSC cell lines (MGG4, MGG6, and MGG8).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: TGF-β signaling controls FMOD expression in glioma.
source: In line with our previous findings indicating that TGF-β signaling controls FMOD expression in glioma (Mondal et al., 2017), we next explored the possible role of this pathway in FMOD overexpression in DGCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Mondal et al., 2017, and by experimental data in the current manuscript showing TGF-β inhibitor effects.

claim: Gene set enrichment analysis shows significant depletion of several TGF-β signaling pathway genes in GSCs compared to DGCs.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of differentially regulated transcripts in GSC vs. DGC showed significant depletion of several TGF-β signaling pathway genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 2), suggesting an enhanced TGF-β signaling in DGCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Enhanced TGF-β signaling occurs in DGCs.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of differentially regulated transcripts in GSC vs. DGC showed significant depletion of several TGF-β signaling pathway genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 2), suggesting an enhanced TGF-β signaling in DGCs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from GSEA data showing depletion of TGF-β pathway genes in GSCs, which suggests enrichment in DGCs.

claim: GSEA reveals enrichment of several TGF-β signaling pathway genes in most GBM transcriptome datasets.
source: Likewise, GSEA revealed an enrichment of several TGF-β signaling pathway genes in most GBM transcriptome datasets (Figure 1—source data 8), further supporting the activation of TGF-β signaling in DGCs that represent the bulk of GBMs.
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis of multiple publicly available GBM datasets.

claim: DGCs used in this study express a high level of FMOD and show enrichment in mesenchymal signature compared to GSCs.
source: In addition, the DGCs used in this study that express a high level of FMOD showed enrichment in mesenchymal signature compared to GSCs (Figure 1—source data 10), consistent with the elevated TGF TGF-β signaling and FMOD levels we observed in the mesenchymal GBM subtype (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A B).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis data shown in Figure 1—source data 10.

claim: Elevated TGF-β signaling and FMOD levels are observed in the mesenchymal GBM subtype.
source: In addition, the DGCs used in this study that express a high level of FMOD showed enrichment in mesenchymal signature compared to GSCs (Figure 1—source data 10), consistent with the elevated TGF TGF-β signaling and FMOD levels we observed in the mesenchymal GBM subtype (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: Treatment with TGF-β inhibitor SB431542 significantly decreases luciferase activity of SBE-Luc reporter in MGG8-DGCs.
source: Moreover, treating MGG8-DGCs with the TGF-β inhibitor (SB431542) significantly decreased luciferase activity of SBE–Luc (a TGF-β-responsive reporter and contains Smad-binding elements) and FMOD Promoter-Luc reporters (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C D).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Treatment with TGF-β inhibitor SB431542 significantly decreases luciferase activity of FMOD Promoter-Luc reporter in MGG8-DGCs.
source: Moreover, treating MGG8-DGCs with the TGF-β inhibitor (SB431542) significantly decreased luciferase activity of SBE–Luc (a TGF-β-responsive reporter and contains Smad-binding elements) and FMOD Promoter-Luc reporters (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C D).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: MGG8-DGCs have higher levels of FMOD and TGM2 transcripts than MGG8-GSCs.
source: We also found higher levels of FMOD and TGM2 (a bonafide TGF-β target gene) transcripts and FMOD and pSMAD2 (an indicator of activated TGF-β signaling) proteins in MGG8-DGCs than MGG8-GSCs (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: MGG8-DGCs have higher levels of FMOD and pSMAD2 proteins than MGG8-GSCs.
source: We also found higher levels of FMOD and TGM2 (a bonafide TGF-β target gene) transcripts and FMOD and pSMAD2 (an indicator of activated TGF-β signaling) proteins in MGG8-DGCs than MGG8-GSCs (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figures 1H and 1I.

claim: Addition of TGF-β inhibitor SB431542 significantly decreases transcript levels of FMOD and TGM2 in MGG8-DGCs.
source: The addition of a TGF-β inhibitor (SB431542) significantly decreased transcript levels of FMOD and TGM2 and protein levels of FMOD and pSMAD2 in MGG8-DGCs (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Addition of TGF-β inhibitor SB431542 significantly decreases protein levels of FMOD and pSMAD2 in MGG8-DGCs.
source: The addition of a TGF-β inhibitor (SB431542) significantly decreased transcript levels of FMOD and TGM2 and protein levels of FMOD and pSMAD2 in MGG8-DGCs (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figures 1H and 1I.

claim: Chromatin immunoprecipitation experiments reveal pSMAD2 occupancy on FMOD promoter in MGG8 DGCs.
source: Further, chromatin immunoprecipitation experiments revealed pSMAD2 occupancy on FMOD promoter in MGG8 DGCs that was significantly reduced by pretreating cells with SB431542 (Figure 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: pSMAD2 occupancy on FMOD promoter in MGG8 DGCs is significantly reduced by pretreatment with SB431542.
source: Further, chromatin immunoprecipitation experiments revealed pSMAD2 occupancy on FMOD promoter in MGG8 DGCs that was significantly reduced by pretreating cells with SB431542 (Figure 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: TGF-β signaling promotes the predominant expression and secretion of FMOD by DGCs.
source: These results demonstrate a predominant expression and secretion of FMOD by DGCs that are promoted by TGF-β signaling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results showing TGF-β pathway activation in DGCs and its effect on FMOD expression.

claim: DBT-Luc-DGCs express higher levels of FMOD than DBT-Luc-GSCs.
source: Reminiscent of our observations in MGG8 cell line, DBT-Luc-DGCs express higher levels of FMOD than DBT-Luc-GSCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 5C D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR and Western blotting data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5C and D.

claim: Tumors in mice coinjected with DBT-Luc-GSCs and DBT-Luc-DGCs/miRNT grew much faster and reached a significantly larger size than tumors in mice injected with DBT-Luc-GSCs alone.
source: Tumors in mice coinjected with DBT-Luc-GSCs and DBT-Luc-DGCs/miRNT grew much faster and reached a significantly larger size (measured by bioluminescence) than tumors in mice injected with DBT-Luc-GSCs alone regardless of doxycycline treatment (Figure 2B–D, compare black and purple lines with blue line; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo bioluminescence imaging data shown in Figures 2B-D.

claim: Injected DBT-Luc-DGC/miRFMOD cells fail to support the growth of tumors initiated by DBT-Luc-GSCs in doxycycline-treated mice compared to doxycycline-untreated mice.
source: In contrast, injected DBT-Luc-DGC/miRFMOD cells failed to support the growth of tumors initiated by DBT-Luc-GSCs in doxycycline-treated mice compared to doxycycline-untreated mice (Figure 2B–D, compare red line with orange line; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo bioluminescence imaging data shown in Figures 2B-D.

claim: Mice injected with DBT-Luc-DGCs alone developed substantially small tumors.
source: As expected, mice injected with DBT-Luc-DGCs alone developed substantially small tumors (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo bioluminescence imaging data shown in Figures 2C and D.

claim: Small tumors formed in animals injected with either DBT-Luc-GSC+DBT-Luc-DGC/miRFMOD (Dox+) or DBT-Luc-GSC alone expressed significantly less FMOD protein than other tumors.
source: The small tumors formed in animals injected with either DBT-Luc-GSC+DBT-Luc-DGC/miRFMOD (Dox+) or DBT-Luc-GSC alone expressed significantly less FMOD protein than other tumors (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: FMOD secreted by DGCs is essential for the growth of tumors initiated by GSCs.
source: These results indicate that FMOD secreted by DGCs is essential for the growth of tumors initiated by GSCs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from co-implantation experiments showing reduced tumor growth when FMOD is silenced in DGCs.

claim: Small leucine-rich proteoglycans such as FMOD promote angiogenesis in the context of cutaneous wound healing.
source: Small leucine-rich proteoglycans such as FMOD promote angiogenesis in the context of cutaneous wound healing (Pang et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Pang et al., 2019 and Zheng et al., 2014.

claim: There is significant enrichment of the term 'angiogenesis' among differentially regulated genes in FMOD-silenced U251 glioma cells.
source: In addition, we previously found a significant enrichment of the term 'angiogenesis' among differentially regulated genes in FMOD-silenced U251 glioma cells (Mondal et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Mondal et al., 2017.

claim: Conditioned medium from LN229 cells stably expressing FMOD induces more angiogenesis than LN229/Vector stable cells.
source: We found that the CM derived from LN229 cells stably expressing FMOD (LN229/FMOD) induced more angiogenesis than LN229/Vector stable cells (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figures 3A and B.

claim: Conditioned medium of FMOD-silenced U251 cells is less efficient in promoting angiogenesis than the CM of cells expressing nontargeting siRNA or shRNA.
source: Further, the CM of FMOD-silenced U251 cells was less efficient in promoting angiogenesis than the CM of cells expressing nontargeting siRNA (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) or shRNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Addition of recombinant human FMOD to the CM of U251/siFMOD cells rescues its ability to induce angiogenesis.
source: The addition of recombinant human FMOD (rhFMOD) to the CM of U251/siFMOD cells rescued its ability to induce angiogenesis (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Addition of rhFMOD directly to endothelial cells induces angiogenesis in the presence of a control antibody (IgG) but not in the presence of an FMOD neutralizing antibody.
source: More importantly, the addition of rhFMOD directly to endothelial cells induced angiogenesis in the presence of a control antibody (IgG) but not in the presence of an FMOD neutralizing antibody ( Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Conditioned media derived from three DGCs and their corresponding GSCs induce angiogenesis efficiently.
source: Both CMs derived from three DGCs and their corresponding GSCs also induced angiogenesis efficiently (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Pretreating cells with an FMOD antibody significantly reduces the ability of MGG8-DGC CM, but not that of MGG8-GSC CM, to induce angiogenesis.
source: Further, pretreating cells with an FMOD antibody significantly reduced the ability of MGG8-DGC CM, but not that of MGG8-GSC CM, to induce angiogenesis (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The reduced ability of FMOD antibody-pretreated DGC CM to promote angiogenesis is rescued by the exogenous addition of an excess of rhFMOD.
source: The reduced ability of the FMOD antibody-pretreated DGC CM to promote angiogenesis was rescued by the exogenous addition of an excess of rhFMOD (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: CM derived from FMOD-silenced MGG8-DGCs is less efficient in promoting angiogenesis than the CM of shNT or siNT transfected MGG-DGCs.
source: Moreover, CM derived from FMOD-silenced MGG8-DGCs was less efficient in promoting angiogenesis than the CM of shNT (Figure 3D) or siNT (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) transfected MGG-DGCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The effect of FMOD silencing on angiogenesis is rescued by adding exogenous rhFMOD.
source: The effect of FMOD silencing was rescued by adding exogenous rhFMOD (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Both rhFMOD and FMOD present in the CM collected from MGG8-DGC induce the migration and invasion but not the proliferation of ST1 cells.
source: Both rhFMOD and FMOD present in the CM collected from MGG8-DGC induced the migration and invasion but not the proliferation of ST1 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Boyden chamber migration and invasion assays and MTT proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-E.

claim: CM from MGG8-DGC/shNT cells is more efficient than CM from MGG8-DGC/shFMOD cells in promoting angiogenic network formation by human brain-derived primary endothelial cells (HBMECs).
source: Further, CM from MGG8-DGC/shNT cells was more efficient than CM from MGG8-DGC/shFMOD cells in promoting angiogenic network formation by human brain-derived primary endothelial cells (HBMECs) and mouse brain-derived immortalized endothelial cells (B.End3) (Figure 3E and F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figures 3E and F.

claim: CM from MGG8-DGC/shNT cells is more efficient than CM from MGG8-DGC/shFMOD cells in promoting angiogenic network formation by mouse brain-derived immortalized endothelial cells (B.End3).
source: Further, CM from MGG8-DGC/shNT cells was more efficient than CM from MGG8-DGC/shFMOD cells in promoting angiogenic network formation by human brain-derived primary endothelial cells (HBMECs) and mouse brain-derived immortalized endothelial cells (B.End3) (Figure 3E and F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F.

claim: The effect of FMOD silencing on angiogenesis by HBMECs and B.End3 cells is rescued by adding rhFMOD.
source: Again, the effect of FMOD silencing was rescued by adding rhFMOD (Figure 3E and F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figures 3E and F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Vascular mimicry is one of the alternative mechanisms of angiogenesis wherein tumor-derived endothelial cells (TDECs) originate from GBM cells.
source: Vascular mimicry (VM) is one of the alternative mechanisms of angiogenesis wherein tumor-derived endothelial cells (TDECs) originate from GBM cells (Angara et al., 2017; Ricci-Vitiani et al., 2010; Soda et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Angara et al., 2017; Ricci-Vitiani et al., 2010; and Soda et al., 2011.

claim: MGG8-DGC/shNT cells grown in endothelial media under hypoxia differentiate to TDECs as evidenced by an increase in CD31.
source: MGG8-DGC/shNT cells grown in endothelial media (M199) under hypoxia (1% O2) differentiated to TDECS as evidenced by an increase in CD31 (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR and Western blotting data shown in Figures 3G and H.

claim: MGG8-DGC/shFMOD also differentiate to form TDECs, albeit with less efficiency than MGG8-DGC/shNT.
source: MGG8-DGC/shFMOD also differentiated to form TDECs, albeit with less efficiency (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR and Western blotting data shown in Figures 3G and H.

claim: Addition of rhFMOD induces both MGG8-DGC/shNT-TDEC and MGG8-DGC/shFMOD-TDEC cells to form angiogenic networks efficiently.
source: Further, the addition of rhFMOD induced both MGG8-DGC/shNT-TDEC and MGG8-DGC/shFMOD-TDEC cells to form angiogenic networks efficiently (Figure 3I and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figures 3I and J.

claim: U87 cells differentiate to TDECs.
source: Similarly, U87 cells differentiated to TDECs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A B), which readily formed angiogenic networks in the presence of rhFMOD (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR and Western blotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: U87-derived TDECs readily form angiogenic networks in the presence of rhFMOD.
source: Similarly, U87 cells differentiated to TDECs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A B), which readily formed angiogenic networks in the presence of rhFMOD (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C and D.

claim: DGC CM can induce angiogenesis.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that DGC CM can induce angiogenesis and identify FMOD as a critical mediator of DGC-induced angiogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple in vitro angiogenesis assay results showing DGC CM induces angiogenesis.

claim: FMOD is a critical mediator of DGC-induced angiogenesis.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that DGC CM can induce angiogenesis and identify FMOD as a critical mediator of DGC-induced angiogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing FMOD silencing or neutralization reduces DGC CM-induced angiogenesis, which is rescued by adding rhFMOD.

claim: A total of 12 proteins exhibit differential abundance in a time-dependent manner in rhFMOD-treated ST1 endothelial cells.
source: A total of 12 proteins exhibited differential abundance in a time-dependent manner in rhFMOD-treated ST1 endothelial cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RPPA data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: HES1 is a downstream target of the Notch signaling pathway that has been shown to promote angiogenesis.
source: These include HES1, a downstream target of the Notch signaling pathway that has been shown to promote angiogenesis (Zhao et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Zhao et al., 2017.

claim: Addition of rhFMOD induces luciferase activity of Notch-dependent CSL-Luc and HES-Luc reporters in ST1 cells but not in gamma-secretase inhibitor (GSI) pretreated cells.
source: The addition of rhFMOD induced luciferase activity of Notch-dependent CSL-Luc and HES-Luc reporters in ST1 cells but not in gamma-secretase inhibitor (GSI; a Notch pathway inhibitor) pretreated cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A B).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Addition of rhFMOD increases HES1 mRNA and protein levels in ST1 cells, an effect abolished by GSI pretreatment of cells.
source: The addition of rhFMOD also increased HES1 mRNA and protein levels in ST1 cells, an effect abolished by GSI pretreatment of cells (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR and Western blotting data shown in Figures 4B and C.

claim: rhFMOD treatment results in the translocation of NICD from the cytosol to the nucleus.
source: rhFMOD treatment also resulted in the translocation of NICD (Notch intracellular domain) from the cytosol to the nucleus, as shown by subcellular fractionation and confocal microscopy (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C D).
evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation and confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: rhFMOD fails to induce angiogenic network formation by GSI-pretreated ST1 cells.
source: Furthermore, rhFMOD failed to induce angiogenic network formation by GSI-pretreated ST1 cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: ST1 cells having a stable expression of NICD show enhanced angiogenic network formation than ST1 vector stable cells.
source: In addition, ST1 cells having a stable expression of NICD (ST1/NICD) showed enhanced angiogenic network formation than ST1 vector stable (ST1/Vector) cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: FMOD present in CM from MGG8-DGCs induces ST1/Vector cells, but not ST1/NICD cells, to form more angiogenic networks.
source: FMOD present in CM from MGG8-DGCs induced ST1/Vector cells, but not ST1/NICD cells, to form more angiogenic networks, suggesting that Notch activation in endothelial cells is an essential step in FMOD-induced angiogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: Notch activation in endothelial cells is an essential step in FMOD-induced angiogenesis.
source: FMOD present in CM from MGG8-DGCs induced ST1/Vector cells, but not ST1/NICD cells, to form more angiogenic networks, suggesting that Notch activation in endothelial cells is an essential step in FMOD-induced angiogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing GSI inhibits FMOD-induced angiogenesis and NICD overexpression enhances angiogenesis independently of FMOD.

claim: RPPA data shows upregulation of pFAK in rhFMOD-treated endothelial cells.
source: The increase in phosphorylated FAK (pFAK, FAK_Py397-R-V; the molecule downstream of integrin signaling) levels in rhFMOD-treated endothelial cells, as shown by RPPA (Figure 4A), also suggested a possible role of integrin signaling in FMOD-induced angiogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by RPPA data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: FMOD activates integrin signaling via type I collagen to engage the FAK-Src-Rho-ROCK pathway and promote the migration of glioma cells.
source: This is consistent with our previous findings indicating that FMOD activates integrin signaling via type I collagen to engage the FAK-Src-Rho-ROCK pathway and promote the migration of glioma cells (Mondal et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Mondal et al., 2017.

claim: Addition of rhFMOD increases pFAK in ST1 cells, but not in cells pretreated with RGD peptide.
source: We first confirmed the activation of integrin signaling by FMOD, as assessed by increased pFAK in rhFMOD-treated ST1 cells, but not in cells pretreated with RGD peptide, an integrin inhibitor (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Addition of RGD peptide inhibits angiogenesis induced by LN229/FMOD CM.
source: The addition of RGD peptide inhibited angiogenesis induced by LN229/FMOD CM (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Angiogenesis induced by LN229/FMOD CM is completely inhibited when ST1 cells are pretreated with inhibitors of FAK or Src.
source: Likewise, angiogenesis induced by LN229/FMOD CM was completely inhibited when ST1 cells were pretreated with inhibitors of FAK (FAKi) or Src (PP2), two signaling molecules downstream of integrin (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: FAK and Src inhibitor treatments strongly reduce the basal level of angiogenesis elicited by the CM of LN229/Vector cells.
source: These treatments also strongly reduced the basal level of angiogenesis elicited by the CM of LN229/Vector cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: An inactive analog of Src inhibitor (PP3), as well as inhibitors of RAC1 and ROCK, fail to inhibit the ability of CM derived from LN229/FMOD cells to induce angiogenesis.
source: In contrast, an inactive analog of Src inhibitor (PP3), as well as inhibitors of RAC1 and ROCK, failed to inhibit the ability of CM derived from LN229/FMOD cells to induce angiogenesis (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The interaction of FMOD with type I collagen is essential for integrin activation.
source: Our previous report also demonstrated that the interaction of FMOD with type I collagen is essential for integrin activation (Mondal et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Mondal et al., 2017.

claim: The C-terminal region of FMOD comprises 11 leucine-rich-repeats (LRRs), of which the 11th repeat binds to type I collagen.
source: The C-terminal region of FMOD comprises 11 leucine-rich-repeats (LRRs), of which the 11th repeat binds to type I collagen (Oldberg et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Oldberg et al., 2007.

claim: A synthetic interfering peptide (RLDGNEIKR) corresponding to the 11th LRR of type 1 collagen, but not a modified peptide (RLDGNQIMR), competes with rhFMOD for binding to type I collagen to activate integrin signaling in glioma cells.
source: A synthetic interfering peptide (RLDGNEIKR) corresponding to the 11thh LRR of type 1 collagen, but not a modified peptide (RLDGNQIMR), competes with rhFMOD for binding to type I collagen to activate integrin signaling in glioma cells (Mondal et al., 2017; Oldberg et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Mondal et al., 2017 and Oldberg et al., 2007.

claim: rhFMOD-induced luciferase activity of CSL-Luc and HES-Luc and angiogenesis by ST1 cells are significantly inhibited by the interfering peptide, but not the modified peptide.
source: Consistent with these findings, rhFMOD-induced luciferase activity of CSL-Luc and HES-Luc (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A B) and angiogenesis by ST1 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C) were significantly inhibited by the interfering peptide, but not the modified peptide, suggesting a crucial role of type I collagen-dependent activation of integrin signaling in FMOD-induced angiogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay and in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A-C.

claim: Type I collagen-dependent activation of integrin signaling plays a crucial role in FMOD-induced angiogenesis.
source: Consistent with these findings, rhFMOD-induced luciferase activity of CSL-Luc and HES-Luc (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A B) and angiogenesis by ST1 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C) were significantly inhibited by the interfering peptide, but not the modified peptide, suggesting a crucial role of type I collagen-dependent activation of integrin signaling in FMOD-induced angiogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing that a peptide that competes with FMOD for binding to type I collagen inhibits FMOD-induced angiogenesis.

claim: Silencing either ITGA6, ITGB1, or ITGAV in ST1 cells significantly reduces the ability of rhFMOD to activate integrin as assessed by reduced pFAK levels.
source: Silencing either of the selected three integrin subunits in ST1 cells reduced significantly the ability of rhFMOD to activate integrin as assessed by reduced pFAK levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D–I), thus demonstrating the involvement of αv/β1 and α6/β1 heterodimeric integrin receptors in FMOD activation of integrin signaling in endothelial cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3D-I.

claim: αv/β1 and α6/β1 heterodimeric integrin receptors are involved in FMOD activation of integrin signaling in endothelial cells.
source: Silencing either of the selected three integrin subunits in ST1 cells reduced significantly the ability of rhFMOD to activate integrin as assessed by reduced pFAK levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D–I), thus demonstrating the involvement of αv/β1 and α6/β1 heterodimeric integrin receptors in FMOD activation of integrin signaling in endothelial cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing that silencing ITGA6, ITGB1, or ITGAV reduces FMOD-induced integrin activation.

claim: Pretreatment of ST1 cells with RGD peptide significantly reduces rhFMOD-elicited CSL-Luc and HES-Luc activation.
source: Pretreatment of ST1 cells with RGD peptide significantly reduced rhFMOD-elicited CSL-Luc and HES-Luc activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E F).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: Pretreatment of cells with FAKi or PP2, but not PP3, significantly reduces rhFMOD-induced CSL-Luc and HES-Luc activity in ST1 cells.
source: Likewise, pretreatment of cells with FAKi or PP2, but not PP3, significantly reduced rhFMOD-induced CSL-Luc and HES-Luc activity in ST1 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A-D.

claim: rhFMOD fails to increase HES1 transcript and protein levels in ST1 cells treated with either RGD peptide, FAKi, or PP2, but not in cells treated with PP3.
source: Further, rhFMOD failed to increase HES1 transcript and protein levels in ST1 cells treated with either RGD peptide, FAKi, or PP2, but not in cells treated with PP3 (Figure 4G and H, Figure 4—figure supplement 4E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR and Western blotting data shown in Figures 4G and H and Figure 4—figure supplement 4E-H.

claim: Addition of rhFMOD induces DLL3 and JAG1 transcripts in ST1 cells.
source: While the addition of rhFMOD induced DLL3 and JAG1 transcripts in ST1 cells, RGD peptide pretreatment abolished JAG1 induction (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A), suggesting that JAG1 might be a potential linking molecule.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5A.

claim: RGD peptide pretreatment abolishes JAG1 induction by rhFMOD in ST1 cells.
source: While the addition of rhFMOD induced DLL3 and JAG1 transcripts in ST1 cells, RGD peptide pretreatment abolished JAG1 induction (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A), suggesting that JAG1 might be a potential linking molecule.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5A.

claim: JAG1 might be a potential linking molecule between integrin and Notch signaling in FMOD-treated endothelial cells.
source: While the addition of rhFMOD induced DLL3 and JAG1 transcripts in ST1 cells, RGD peptide pretreatment abolished JAG1 induction (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A), suggesting that JAG1 might be a potential linking molecule.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing JAG1 is induced by FMOD in an integrin-dependent manner.

claim: Pretreatment of cells with either FAKi or PP2, but not PP3, abolishes the ability of rhFMOD to induce JAG1 transcript in ST1 cells.
source: Consistently, pretreatment of cells with either FAKi or PP2, but not PP3, also abolished the ability of rhFMOD to induce JAG1 transcript in ST1 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 5B C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5B and C.

claim: JAG1 silencing significantly decreases rhFMOD-induced activity of CSL-Luc and HES-Luc reporters and HES1 transcript/protein levels in ST1 cells.
source: Further, JAG1 silencing significantly decreased rhFMOD-induced activity of CSL-Luc and HES-Luc reporters and HES1 transcript/protein levels in ST1 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 5D E, Figure 4I–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay, RT-qPCR, and Western blotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5D and E and Figures 4I-K.

claim: JAG1 silencing abolishes the ability of rhFMOD to induce angiogenic networks by ST1 cells.
source: JAG1 silencing also abolished the ability of rhFMOD to induce angiogenic networks by ST1 cells (Figure 4L).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: rhFMOD induces the transcript levels of KLF8, a FAK-inducible transcription factor in ST1 cells, but not in RGD peptide pretreated cells.
source: In addition, rhFMOD induced the transcript levels of KLF8, a FAK-inducible transcription factor in ST1 cells, but not in RGD peptide pretreated cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5F.

claim: KLF8 silencing in ST1 cells significantly reduces the ability of rhFMOD to increase JAG1 level.
source: Further, KLF8 silencing in ST1 cells significantly reduced the ability of rhFMOD to increase JAG1 level (Figure 4—figure supplement 5G H), suggesting that KLF8 activates JAG1 through an integrin-dependent pathway in FMOD-treated endothelial cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5G and H.

claim: KLF8 activates JAG1 through an integrin-dependent pathway in FMOD-treated endothelial cells.
source: Further, KLF8 silencing in ST1 cells significantly reduced the ability of rhFMOD to increase JAG1 level (Figure 4—figure supplement 5G H), suggesting that KLF8 activates JAG1 through an integrin-dependent pathway in FMOD-treated endothelial cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing KLF8 is induced by FMOD in an integrin-dependent manner and KLF8 silencing reduces JAG1 induction by FMOD.

claim: JAG1 is a molecular link between integrin and Notch signaling pathways in FMOD-treated endothelial cells.
source: Collectively, these results identify JAG1 as a molecular link between integrin and Notch signaling pathways in FMOD-treated endothelial cells and demonstrate a key role of integrin-FAK-JAG1-Notch-HES1 signaling in FMOD-induced angiogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing JAG1 is induced by FMOD via integrin-FAK signaling and JAG1 is required for FMOD-induced Notch activation and angiogenesis.

claim: Integrin-FAK-JAG1-Notch-HES1 signaling plays a key role in FMOD-induced angiogenesis.
source: Collectively, these results identify JAG1 as a molecular link between integrin and Notch signaling pathways in FMOD-treated endothelial cells and demonstrate a key role of integrin-FAK-JAG1-Notch-HES1 signaling in FMOD-induced angiogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing each component of this pathway is required for FMOD-induced angiogenesis.

claim: There is significant upregulation of transcript levels of FMOD, JAG1, and HES1 in GBM from various datasets.
source: We found a significant upregulation of transcript levels of FMOD, JAG1, and HES1 in GBM from various datasets (Figure 4—figure supplement 6A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of multiple publicly available GBM transcriptome datasets shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6A-C.

claim: There is a positive correlation between FMOD and HES1 transcripts in the majority of GBM datasets analyzed.
source: We also found a positive correlation between FMOD and HES1 transcripts and between FMOD and JAG1 transcripts in the majority of GBM datasets analyzed (Figure 4—figure supplement 6D E), which further substantiates the functional link between FMOD, JAG1, and HES1.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of multiple publicly available GBM transcriptome datasets shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6D and E.

claim: There is a positive correlation between FMOD and JAG1 transcripts in the majority of GBM datasets analyzed.
source: We also found a positive correlation between FMOD and HES1 transcripts and between FMOD and JAG1 transcripts in the majority of GBM datasets analyzed (Figure 4—figure supplement 6D E), which further substantiates the functional link between FMOD, JAG1, and HES1.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of multiple publicly available GBM transcriptome datasets shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6D and E.

claim: High FMOD transcript levels are associated with poor prognosis in most datasets.
source: We also show that high FMOD transcript levels and hypomethylation of FMOD promoter are associated with poor prognosis in most datasets (Figure 4—figure supplement 7A B).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival analysis of multiple publicly available GBM datasets shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 7A.

claim: Hypomethylation of FMOD promoter is associated with poor prognosis in most datasets.
source: We also show that high FMOD transcript levels and hypomethylation of FMOD promoter are associated with poor prognosis in most datasets (Figure 4—figure supplement 7A B).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival analysis of multiple publicly available GBM datasets shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 7B.

claim: AGR53-GSC-miRNT and AGR53-GSC-miRFMOD cell-initiated tumors show similar size 7 days after doxycycline treatment.
source: AGR53-GSC/miRNT and AGR53-GSC/miRFMOD cell-initiated tumors showed a similar size 7 days after doxycycline treatment as shown by mCherry fluorescence (Figure 5B and C; day 21).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo fluorescence imaging data shown in Figures 5B and C.

claim: Doxycycline administration significantly inhibits the growth of AGR53-GSC/miRFMOD-initiated tumors over time but not that of AGR53-GSC/miRNT tumors.
source: However, upon subsequent follow-up, doxycycline administration significantly inhibited the growth of AGR53-GSC/miRFMOD-initiated tumors over time but not that of AGR53-GSC/miRNT tumors (Figure 5B, C and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo fluorescence imaging and histology data shown in Figures 5B, C, and E.

claim: Doxycycline administration increases the survival of mice injected with AGR53-GSC/miRFMOD cells compared to AGR53-GSC/miRNT cells.
source: Further, doxycycline administration increased the survival of mice injected with AGR53-GSC/miRFMOD cells compared to AGR53-GSC/miRNT cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: AGR53-GSC/miRFMOD-initiated tumors show decreased FMOD, mCherry, and GFP expression compared to AGR53-GSC/miRNT-initiated tumors.
source: AGR53-GSC/miRFMOD-initiated tumors showed decreased FMOD, mCherry, and GFP expression compared to AGR53-GSC/miRNT-initiated tumors (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figures 5F and G.

claim: FMOD silencing after doxycycline administration in DBT-Luc GSC/miRFMOD cells results in reduced tumor growth.
source: DBT-Luc GSC/miRFMOD, another murine glioma GSC cell line, produced similar results: FMOD silencing after doxycycline administration resulted in reduced tumor growth (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A B), increased mice survival (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and decreased FMOD expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo bioluminescence and fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: FMOD silencing after doxycycline administration in DBT-Luc GSC/miRFMOD cells increases mice survival.
source: DBT-Luc GSC/miRFMOD, another murine glioma GSC cell line, produced similar results: FMOD silencing after doxycycline administration resulted in reduced tumor growth (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A B), increased mice survival (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and decreased FMOD expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: FMOD silencing after doxycycline administration in DBT-Luc GSC/miRFMOD cells decreases FMOD expression.
source: DBT-Luc GSC/miRFMOD, another murine glioma GSC cell line, produced similar results: FMOD silencing after doxycycline administration resulted in reduced tumor growth (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A B), increased mice survival (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and decreased FMOD expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Higher expression of CD133 confirms the enrichment of CSCs in MGG8-GSC neurospheres compared to MGG8-DGCs.
source: The higher expression of CD133 confirmed the enrichment of CSCs in MGG8-GSC neurospheres compared to MGG8-DGCs (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: MGG8-GSC/shNT-transplanted mice readily develop intracranial tumors, whereas MGG8-GSC/shFMOD mice show impaired tumor formation and increased mice survival.
source: Reminiscent of results obtained using transplantation of murine glioma cells, MGG8-GSC/shNT-transplanted mice readily developed intracranial tumors, whereas MGG8-GSC/shFMOD mice showed impaired tumor formation and increased mice survival (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and histology data shown in Figures 6B and C.

claim: MGG8-GSC/shNT tumors show high expression of FMOD, while FMOD is barely detectable in MGG8-GSC/shFMOD tumors.
source: Immunostaining and confocal microscopy analysis showed high expression of FMOD in MGG8-GSC/shNT tumors, while FMOD was barely detectable in MGG8-GSC/shFMOD tumors (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: U251/shFMOD cells develop smaller tumors, and mice bearing U251/shFMOD tumors have longer survival than those carrying U251/shNT tumors.
source: Likewise, U251/shFMOD cells that showed reduced FMOD protein levels compared to U251/shNT (Figure 2—figure supplement 6A) developed smaller tumors, and mice bearing U251/shFMOD tumors had longer survival than those carrying U251/shNT tumors (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo bioluminescence imaging, Kaplan-Meier survival analysis, and histology data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: FMOD expression is more elevated in U251/shNT tumors than in U251/shFMOD tumors.
source: As expected, the expression of FMOD was more elevated in U251/shNT tumors than in U251/shFMOD tumors (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: DGC-secreted FMOD is essential for the growth of both human and mouse glioma.
source: Collectively, these findings indicate that DGC-secreted FMOD is essential for the growth of both human and mouse glioma.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple in vivo experiments showing FMOD silencing reduces tumor growth in both human and mouse glioma models.

claim: CD133-positive cells are much less in proportion compared to GFAP-positive cells in tumors formed by AGR53-GSC, DBT-Luc-GSCs, and MGG8-GSCs under FMOD nontargeting conditions.
source: The CD133-positive cells are much less in proportion compared to GFAP-positive cells in tumors formed by AGR53-GSC, DBT-Luc-GSCs, and MGG8-GSCs under FMOD nontargeting conditions (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A B, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A B, Figure 7—figure supplement 3A B), in good correlation to the low proportion of GSCs seen in brain tumors (Singh et al., 2004; Galli et al., 2004; Calabrese et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and B, and Figure 7—figure supplement 3A and B, and citations to previous work.

claim: Most GFAP-positive cells are also positive for FMOD expression compared to CD133-positive cells in tumors.
source: Further, most GFAP-positive cells are also positive for FMOD expression compared to CD133-positive cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A C, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A C, Figure 7—figure supplement 3A C), recapitulating the results we obtained in vitro, where FMOD is expressed specifically by DGCs (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing colocalization of FMOD with GFAP in tumor sections.

claim: Similar expression pattern of CD133 and GFAP markers is found in small tumors formed under FMOD-silenced conditions in all three tumor models.
source: We also found a similar expression pattern of CD133 and GFAP markers in small tumors formed under FMOD-silenced conditions in all three tumor models (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D E, Figure 7—figure supplement 2D E, Figure 7—figure supplement 3D E).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and E, Figure 7—figure supplement 2D and E, and Figure 7—figure supplement 3D and E.

claim: GFAP staining in tumors formed under FMOD-silenced conditions confirms the occurrence of an efficient differentiation program even in FMOD-silenced conditions.
source: The GFAP staining in these tumors confirms the occurrence of an efficient differentiation program even in FMOD-silenced conditions, which confirms our results obtained in vitro, where the absence of FMOD failed to affect the GSC differentiation to form DGCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is inferred from GFAP staining data in tumors and in vitro differentiation experiments.

claim: Small tumors formed in FMOD-silenced conditions show substantially reduced FMOD staining.
source: As expected, the small tumors formed in FMOD-silenced conditions showed substantially reduced FMOD staining (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D F, Figure 7—figure supplement 2D F, Figure 7—figure supplement 3D F).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and F, Figure 7—figure supplement 2D and F, and Figure 7—figure supplement 3D and F.

claim: Small size tumors formed by AGR53-GSC/miRFMOD cells after doxycycline treatment show reduced staining for CD31 and von Willebrand factor (vWF) compared to AGR53-GSC/miRNT tumors.
source: The small size tumors formed by AGR53-GSC/miRFMOD cells after doxycycline treatment showed reduced staining for CD31 and von Willebrand factor (vWF) compared to AGR53-GSC/miRNT tumors (Figure 7A-C, Figure 7—figure supplement 4A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figures 7A-C and Figure 7—figure supplement 4A-C.

claim: Tumors formed by DBT-Luc-GSC/miRFMOD cells in doxycycline-treated mice show significantly reduced CD31 staining compared to that measured in the absence of doxycycline treatment.
source: Tumors formed by DBT-Luc-GSC/miRFMOD cells in doxycycline-treated mice also showed significantly reduced CD31 staining compared to that measured in the absence of doxycycline treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 4D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4D-F.

claim: Tumors induced by MGG8-GSC/shFMOD cells show reduced CD31 staining compared to MGG8-GSC/shNT cells.
source: Reminiscent of murine glioma tumors, tumors induced by MGG8-GSC/shFMOD cells also showed reduced CD31 staining compared to MGG8-GSC/shNT cells (Figure 7D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figures 7D-F.

claim: In all three tumor models (AGR53-GSCs, DBT-Luc-GSCs, and MGG8-GSCs), blood vessels formed by TDECs are significantly reduced in tumors formed in FMOD-silenced conditions.
source: We then tested the extent of blood vessel formation by TDECs. In all three tumor models (AGR53-GSCs, DBT-Luc-GSCs, and MGG8-GSCs), blood vessels formed by TDECs were significantly reduced in tumors formed in FMOD-silenced conditions (Figure 7G–L, Figure 7—figure supplement 4G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing colocalization of CD31 with GFP or GFAP in tumor sections, shown in Figures 7G-L and Figure 7—figure supplement 4G-I.

claim: Confocal microscopy analysis in tumors formed by AGR53-GSCs, DBT-Luc-GSCs, and MGG8-GSCs reveals significant colocalization of the endothelial cell marker CD31 with FMOD, pFAK, JAG1, and HES1 markers in blood vessels.
source: Next, we investigated the involvement of integrin-FAK-JAG1-Notch-HES1 signaling in FMOD-induced angiogenesis in the context of glioma tumors. Confocal microscopy analysis in tumors formed by AGR53-GSCs, DBT-Luc-GSCs, and MGG8-GSCs revealed a significant colocalization of the endothelial cell marker CD31 with FMOD, pFAK, JAG1, and HES1 markers in blood vessels (Figure 7—figure supplement 5A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 5A-C.

claim: Angiogenesis induced by DGC-secreted FMOD is essential for glioma tumor growth.
source: From these results, we conclude that angiogenesis induced by DGC-secreted FMOD is essential for glioma tumor growth.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing FMOD silencing reduces angiogenesis and tumor growth in vivo.

claim: Tumor-initiating capacity lies solely with CSCs.
source: It is well established that the tumor-initiating capacity lies solely with CSCs, thereby making them the crucial architects of tumor–stroma interactions that favor tumor growth and progression (Rheinbay et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Rheinbay et al., 2013.

claim: CSCs are capable of self-renewal and give rise to differentiated cells that form the bulk of the tumor.
source: CSCs have a dichotomous division pattern as they are capable of self-renewal and give rise to differentiated cells that form the bulk of the tumor (Olmeda and Ben Amar, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Olmeda and Ben Amar, 2019.

claim: The indispensable role of CSCs is well documented in many solid tumors.
source: The indispensable role of CSCs, which usually constitute only a minority population within tumors, is well documented in many solid tumors (Galli et al., 2004; Ignatova et al., 2002; Singh et al., 2004; Yang et al., 2020a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Galli et al., 2004; Ignatova et al., 2002; Singh et al., 2004; and Yang et al., 2020a.

claim: The tumor microenvironment is a vital driver of plasticity and heterogeneity in cancer.
source: The tumor microenvironment is a vital driver of plasticity and heterogeneity in cancer (Carnero and Lleonart, 2016; Heddleston et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Carnero and Lleonart, 2016 and Heddleston et al., 2010.

claim: The presence of hypoxic and necrotic regions is the hallmark of very aggressive tumors like glioblastoma (GBM).
source: The presence of hypoxic and necrotic regions is the hallmark of very aggressive tumors like glioblastoma (GBM), which have a highly vascular niche that supplies nutrients to cancer cells and makes a conducive environment for the tumor cells to thrive (Hambardzumyan and Bergers, 2015; Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Hambardzumyan and Bergers, 2015 and Huang et al., 2016.

claim: Paracrine signaling mediated by proteins secreted from tumor cells, particularly glioma stem-like cells (GSCs), helps acquire a highly vascular phenotype by attracting blood vessels and inducing pro-angiogenic signaling in endothelial cells through extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling.
source: Paracrine signaling mediated by proteins secreted from tumor cells, particularly glioma stem-like cells (GSCs), helps acquire this highly vascular phenotype by attracting blood vessels and inducing pro-angiogenic signaling in endothelial cells through extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling (Dittmer and Leyh, 2014; Rupp et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Dittmer and Leyh, 2014 and Rupp et al., 2016.

claim: A reciprocal relationship exists between GSCs and endothelial cells by which endothelial cells induce stemness phenotype in cancer cells through activation of Notch, sonic hedgehog (SHH), and nitric oxide synthase signaling pathways.
source: A reciprocal relationship exists between GSCs and endothelial cells by which endothelial cells induce stemness phenotype in cancer cells through activation of Notch, sonic hedgehog (SHH), and nitric oxide synthase signaling pathways (Jeon et al., 2014; Yan et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2011), while GSCs drive vascularization of the tumor via endogenous endothelial cell stimulation, vascular mimicry, and GBM-endothelial cell transdifferentiation (Hardee and Zagzag, 2012; Soda et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Jeon et al., 2014; Yan et al., 2014; and Zhu et al., 2011.

claim: GSCs drive vascularization of the tumor via endogenous endothelial cell stimulation, vascular mimicry, and GBM-endothelial cell transdifferentiation.
source: A reciprocal relationship exists between GSCs and endothelial cells by which endothelial cells induce stemness phenotype in cancer cells through activation of Notch, sonic hedgehog (SHH), and nitric oxide synthase signaling pathways (Jeon et al., 2014; Yan et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2011), while GSCs drive vascularization of the tumor via endogenous endothelial cell stimulation, vascular mimicry, and GBM-endothelial cell transdifferentiation (Hardee and Zagzag, 2012; Soda et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Hardee and Zagzag, 2012 and Soda et al., 2011.

claim: CSCs induce high vascularization of tumors like GBM by migrating along blood vessel scaffolds to invade novel vascular niches.
source: Recent reports have shown that CSCs induce high vascularization of tumors like GBM by migrating along blood vessel scaffolds to invade novel vascular niches, thereby ensuring surplus and continuous blood supply at their disposal (Prager et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Prager et al., 2020.

claim: In GBM, CD133+ and Nestin+ cells (representing GSCs) are located in close proximity to the tumor microvascular density (MVD), whereas a lower number of CD133- and Nestin- cells (representing differentiated glioma cells [DGCs]) are located in the vicinity of the blood vessels.
source: In GBM, CD133+ and Nestin+ cells (representing GSCs) are located in close proximity to the tumor microvascular density (MVD), whereas a lower number of CD133- and Nestin- cells (representing differentiated glioma cells [DGCs]) are located in the vicinity of the blood vessels.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge without a specific citation in this sentence, but is supported by the citation to Calabrese et al., 2007 in the next sentence.

claim: Depletion of brain tumor blood vessels causes a decrease in the number of tumor-initiating GSCs.
source: It has also been reported that the depletion of brain tumor blood vessels causes a decrease in the number of tumor-initiating GSCs (Calabrese et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Calabrese et al., 2007.

claim: CD133 marker expression was initially reported to be associated with GSCs.
source: While CD133 marker expression was reported to be associated with GSCs initially (Singh et al., 2004; Galli et al., 2004), later reports documented CD133- cells exhibiting GSC-like properties (Beier et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2010; Joo et al., 2008; Ogden et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Singh et al., 2004 and Galli et al., 2004.

claim: Later reports documented CD133- cells exhibiting GSC-like properties.
source: While CD133 marker expression was reported to be associated with GSCs initially (Singh et al., 2004; Galli et al., 2004), later reports documented CD133- cells exhibiting GSC-like properties (Beier et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2010; Joo et al., 2008; Ogden et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Beier et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2010; Joo et al., 2008; Ogden et al., 2008; and Wang et al., 2008.

claim: CXCR4-dependent SHH-GLI-NANOG signaling promotes stemness in GSCs.
source: CXCR4-dependent SHH-GLI-NANOG signaling promotes stemness in GSCs. This study also showed that the miR302-367 cluster could suppress stemness and promote differentiation by targeting CXCR4/SDF1 (Fareh et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Fareh et al., 2012.

claim: The miR302-367 cluster can suppress stemness and promote differentiation by targeting CXCR4/SDF1.
source: CXCR4-dependent SHH-GLI-NANOG signaling promotes stemness in GSCs. This study also showed that the miR302-367 cluster could suppress stemness and promote differentiation by targeting CXCR4/SDF1 (Fareh et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Fareh et al., 2012.

claim: miR18A* promotes GSC stemness by activating Notch-dependent SHH-GL1-NANOG signaling, targeting DLL3, an autocrine inhibitor of Notch 1 signaling.
source: The above group subsequently showed that miR18A* promotes GSC stemness by activating Notch-dependent SHH-GL1-NANOG signaling, targeting DLL3, an autocrine inhibitor of Notch 1 signaling (Turchi et al., 2013).
